Containerized Big Data Architecture¶

Charles Wainright

2026-08-07

Introduction¶

This project implements a fully containerized big data architecture designed to ingest, process, and analyze distributed financial datasets at scale. The underlying dataset originates from a MongoDB collection of historical stock transactions containing millions of records detailing company names, symbols, continuous pricing metrics, and precise transaction timestamps.

To execute this pipeline, we deployed a robust multi-node technology stack combining Docker for containerization, a replicated MongoDB NoSQL cluster for high-availability data storage, Apache Spark (PySpark) for distributed data processing, and JupyterLab as an interactive analytical environment. Using this architecture, we established a containerized replica set, performed rigorous data wrangling and type-casting on high-frequency transaction logs, engineered true time-based moving averages over a 30-day window, and queried the distributed datasets to generate and visualize actionable financial insights.

Environment¶

Docker¶

I used Docker Desktop, which gave me access to both the Docker CLI and a GUI program to manage containers. https://docs.docker.com/desktop/setup/install/windows-install

Then, I installed the Windows Subsystem for Linux to run Docker.

In [ ]:
{shell}
wsl --install

Finally, I ran the following Docker shell commands (https://github.com/RWaltersMA/mongo-spark-jupyter/tree/master). The commands start new containers, initialize a MongoDB cluster, and then seed the cluster's Stocks database with data from Source.bson.

In [ ]:
{shell}
docker-compose up -d --build
In [ ]:
{shell}
docker-compose exec mongo1 /usr/bin/mongo --eval "if (rs.status()['ok'] == 0) { rsconf = { _id : 'rs0', members: [ { _id : 0, host : 'mongo1:27017', priority: 1.0 }, { _id : 1, host : 'mongo2:27017', priority: 0.5 }, { _id : 2, host : 'mongo3:27017', priority: 0.5 } ] }; rs.initiate(rsconf); } rs.conf();"
In [ ]:
{shell}
docker-compose exec mongo1 apt-get update
In [ ]:
{shell}
docker-compose exec mongo1 apt-get install wget
In [ ]:
{shell}
docker-compose exec mongo1 wget https://github.com/RWaltersMA/mongo-spark-jupyter/raw/master/Source.bson
In [ ]:
{shell}
docker-compose exec mongo1 /usr/bin/mongorestore Source.bson -h rs0/mongo1:27017,mongo2:27018,mongo3:27019 -d Stocks -c Source --drop
In [ ]:
{shell}
docker exec -it mongo1 mongorestore --db=Stocks --collection=Source Source.bson

Confirm Docker¶

I confirmed the health and completeness of my Docker containers with the following shell command which shows me each container in Docker and the container's status.

In [ ]:
{shell}
docker ps

Confirm Spark¶

To confirm that Spark was running in my container, I visited http://localhost:8090/, which was the port specified for Spark in my docker-compose.yml file.

Confirm MongoDB¶

I confirmed that MongoDB was running and populated with data with the following shell commands. I first queried MongoDB to ask for the name of all databases in my container. Then, I queried my Stocks database to determine how many rows it contained.

In [ ]:
{shell}
docker exec -it mongo1 mongosh --eval "show dbs"
docker exec -it mongo1 mongosh Stocks --eval "db.Source.countDocuments()"

Python¶

I spun up a jupyterlab instance in my project's docker container.

In [ ]:
{shell}
docker exec -it jupyterlab  /opt/conda/bin/jupyter server list

Then I navigated to http://localhost:8888/ in my web browser to begin my jupyter session.

Data Transformation¶

Spark Session¶

First I connected Spark to my MongoDB via a SparkSession.

In [53]:
# If needed
# !pip install pyspark
In [1]:
import plotly.express as px
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.\
        builder.\
        appName("big_data").\
        master("local[*]").\
        config("spark.mongodb.input.uri", "mongodb://mongo1:27017,mongo2:27018,mongo3:27019/Stocks.Source?replicaSet=rs0").\
        config("spark.mongodb.output.uri", "mongodb://mongo1:27017,mongo2:27018,mongo3:27019/Stocks.Source?replicaSet=rs0").\
        config("spark.jars.packages", "org.mongodb.spark:mongo-spark-connector_2.12:3.0.0").\
        getOrCreate()

df = spark.read.format("mongo").load()

Next, I confirmed that my connection was valid by printing the data schema.

In [2]:
df.printSchema()

 |-- company_symbol: string (nullable = true)
 |-- movingAverage: double (nullable = true)

 |-- tx_time: timestamp (nullable = true)

Querying: WHERE¶

I used the filter() method to filter the dataset to return only rows where the price was less than or equal to $20.

.filter(

)\
.select('company','price')\

Querying: CASE¶

Next, I created a column called recent and wrote a case statement to populate the column with a 1 when the tx_time column was greater than or equal to noon on 2026-06-01.

In [46]:
df.select('company', 'price', 
            when(col("tx_time") >= lit("2026-06-01 12:00:00"), 1).otherwise(0).alias('recent')
           ).toPandas()\
.head(5).style \

Bar Chart¶

I created a bar chart to show the average price of each of the 10 most-expensive companies.

In [20]:
# 1. Perform your PySpark grouping and aggregation
avg_price_df = df.groupBy("company_symbol") \
                 .avg("price") \
                 .orderBy("avg(price)", ascending=False) \
                 .limit(10)

# 2. Convert the Spark DataFrame into a local Pandas DataFrame using .toPandas()
pandas_df = avg_price_df.toPandas()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ax = pandas_df.plot(kind='bar', x='company_symbol', y='avg(price)', color='steelblue', figsize=(8, 5))
plt.title("Top 10 Companies by Average Stock Price", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.xlabel("Company Symbol", fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel("Average Price ($)", fontsize=12)
plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Moving Average¶

To evaluate underlying market trends without short-term market noise, I constructed a time-based window frame spanning 30 days of seconds and compute a rolling average of transaction prices grouped by company symbol.

In [32]:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Define a time-based window: 30 days behind the current row's timestamp up to the current row
window_30day = Window.partitionBy("company_symbol") \
                     .orderBy(F.col("tx_time").cast("long")) \
                     .rangeBetween(-2592000, 0)

# Calculate the 30-day moving average
movAvg = df.withColumn("movingAverage30day", F.avg("price").over(window_30day))
In [44]:
movAvg\
.select('company','tx_time','movingAverage30day')\
.toPandas()\
.head(5).style \
    .format({"movingAverage30day": "${:.2f}"}) \
    .background_gradient(subset=["movingAverage30day"], cmap="Blues") \
    .set_table_styles([
        {"selector": "th", "props": [("background-color", "#2c3e50"), ("color", "white"), ("font-weight", "bold"), ("padding", "8px")]},
        {"selector": "td", "props": [("padding", "8px")]}
    ]) \
    .hide(axis="index")
Out[44]:

I plotted the high-frequency transaction prices alongside our 30-day moving average time-series, mapping clean date-formatted axes to clearly highlight historical valuation trends.

In [34]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import pandas as pd

# 1. Filter and convert to Pandas (ensuring tx_time is recognized as a datetime)
company_df = movAvg.filter(movAvg.company_symbol == "IAC") \
                  .orderBy("tx_time") \
                  .toPandas()

# Ensure the column is explicitly a datetime type
company_df["tx_time"] = pd.to_datetime(company_df["tx_time"])

# 2. Build the Matplotlib figure
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

plt.plot(
    company_df["tx_time"], 
    company_df["price"], 
    label="Raw Price", 
    color="lightblue", 
    marker="o", 
    markersize=3, 
    linestyle="-"
)

plt.plot(
    company_df["tx_time"], 
    company_df["movingAverage30day"], 
    label="30-day Simple Moving Average", 
    color="darkblue", 
    linewidth=2, 
    linestyle="--"
)

# 3. Format the X-Axis to display as yyyy-mm-dd
plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter('%Y-%m-%d'))
# Optional: Adjust locator frequency if labels crowd together (e.g., auto-locate ticks)
plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.AutoDateLocator())

# Rotate date labels slightly so they don't overlap
plt.xticks(rotation=30)

# 4. Add styling, labels, and legend
plt.title("Stock Price & Moving Average Over Time: IAC", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
plt.xlabel("Transaction Date", fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel("Price ($)", fontsize=12)
plt.grid(True, linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)
plt.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.tight_layout()

plt.show()

Once I was satisfied that my moving average was correct, I saved the output to the database.

In [35]:
movAvg.write.format("mongo").option("replaceDocument", "true").mode("append").save()

Pipelines and Views¶

PySpark Pipelines¶

Next I created a pipeline that filtered, sorted, and aggregated data. The pipeline creates a repeatable summary that shows each company's maximum price. A summary like this might be useful in reporting.

In [40]:
pipeline = "[{'$group': {_id:'$company', 'maxprice': {$max:'$price'}}},{$sort:{'maxprice':-1}}]"
aggPipelineDF = spark.read.format("mongo").option("pipeline", pipeline).option("partitioner", "MongoSinglePartitioner").load()
aggPipelineDF.toPandas().head(5)
Out[40]:
_id maxprice
0 FRUSTRATING CHAOS LLC 87.60
1 HOMELY KIOSK UNLIMITED 86.48
2 CREEPY GIT HOLDINGS 83.40
3 GREASY CHAMPION CORPORATION 81.76
4 COMBATIVE TOWNSHIP LLC 72.18

ANSI-compliant SQL¶

Then I created a view in ANSI-compliant SQL to find records where the moving average was > $43.

In [43]:
movAvg.createOrReplaceTempView("avgs")
sqlDF=spark.sql("SELECT * FROM avgs WHERE movingAverage30day > 43.0")
sqlDF.toPandas().head(5)

Export views¶

To ensure broad interoperability and support downstream delivery requirements, the final analytical views are exported into CSV, JSON, and Parquet formats.

In [ ]:
# CSV
sqlDF.write.csv("sqlview.csv")
aggPipelineDF.write.csv("pipeline.csv")

# JSON
sqlDF.write.save("sqlview.json", format="json")
aggPipelineDF.write.save("pipeline.json", format="json")

# Parquet
sqlDF.write.save("sqlview.parquet", format="parquet")
aggPipelineDF.write.save("pipeline.parquet", format="parquet")
